questions.knowledge_point: Classifying Decoupled Systems of Linear Differential Equations
questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Select the correct options below regarding the given decoupled system of linear differential equations.$\,$
The $x$-axis is a {{field-1}} line.

$\,$
The $y$-axis is a {{field-2}} line.

$\,$
The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis and approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a saddle point}.$ 

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14076662/assets/0948dac4f8a192018baee1339d7334d573592d7b7bf4383c1297cc2431e51201.png)

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the System Given a Phase Portrait
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14076662/assets/98ffa8fec669ce09d22b5b904b710632314f7b22e0eb5098719c41147c186975.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?
questions.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}>0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Phase Portrait Given a System: Advanced Cases
questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-4t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14076662/assets/3fdbeba46a0f4640e909b0ba489c1aec1fa87a6aa7740f19d08f274b7351d11b.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-3t})^{′}}=\frac{-4{c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}}{-3{c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}}{3{c}_{1}}{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14076662/assets/4193300af5a8950ce70e2c469812424235665faac279dac0c89289a0307ab46a.png)
